title: Coffin Baby
intro: The song follows a performer whose need for approval makes him available to be used. Admiration, money and pleasure become bodily exposure; praise keeps feeding his conceit after pleasure has stopped satisfying him. Then the voice of the seller takes over and explains how cornering this person makes money. Jack also puts 'my head' into the opening burial image, so the contempt never belongs safely outside the situation. This is a grotesque account of performing for validation, not just a collection of death jokes. Even the final refusal to believe anybody loops back into asking whether he is impressive.
reading: The circulation of performer, consumer and exploiter roles; self-implication and a circular appetite for validation.

revisions.5-swagger: The question asks another person to certify his greatness. Its repetition makes that need audible, and 'bury my head' briefly places the first-person speaker among the song's future dead. He is not securely outside the fate he goes on to mock in 'you.' By the ending, after dismissing everyone's words as bullshit, he returns to the same request for a verdict. That loop matters: recognizing flattery as poisonous has not removed the wish to hear it. The song's performer is trapped partly by what he wants from the audience.
revisions.editorial-5-parasite: The sequence distinguishes conceit from desire. The ego is still growing inside the performer while the capacity to enjoy anything is disappearing: he has already had everything, and now he is bored. Praise can keep the inflated image alive after the person it supposedly rewards has become empty. That is why the medical imagery belongs to the fame story rather than interrupting it. The performer is not simply punished for wanting success; the promised reward fails to nourish him, while the appetite for more approval survives.
revisions.editorial-5-soaking: To 'spend the rest of your life' usually promises companionship. Here the companion is other people's insincere praise. The image makes applause into an environment you cannot leave, even when it no longer gives pleasure. The next movement—from naivety to everybody trampling him—shows how little protection that environment provides. The same social attention that seemed to hold him up can turn into a crowd acting on his body. The song is describing dependence on an audience whose tenderness was never dependable.
revisions.editorial-5-forced-desire: This is the song's clearest statement of the trap: it is no longer enough to buy the package or obey the instructions; he must appear to want what everybody wants for him. The package is a coffin and funeral clothes, which makes the demand for consent grotesque. The following commands require obscenity during ritual and a grin during crying. All three instructions erase the difference between a person's actual feelings and the performance that others find useful. The offer of a choice becomes another way to dictate the answer.
revisions.editorial-5-cry-grin: The explanation arrives two lines later: 'so I can make money.' That first-person voice is now openly profiting from the other person's desperation. It is a shift in position, not simply the artist narrating someone else's bad business practices. After speaking as the performer and attacking him, the song can also ventriloquize the person squeezing value out of him. The forced grin is the product: pain has to remain entertaining and saleable. Hearing that change of voice makes the verse much more specific than a general warning that fame is dangerous.
revisions.phrase-5-bullshit: After offers, compliments and commands have all been exposed as ways of extracting something, the response is to reject speech wholesale: do not trust anybody, do not listen to anybody. But the song does not end with that achieved independence. It returns to 'tell me, am I impressive?' and repeats the account of boredom and conceit. The refusal is therefore a moment inside the trap rather than a clean escape from it. He can recognize the mechanism and still be pulled back into asking the audience for the thing that sustains it.
